sessions.notes:
- There is NO category column. World / Sports / Business / Science/Technology must be inferred from `agnews_articles.title` + `description` (the AG News corpus). `doc` is just a JSON copy of those two fields.
- Joins are clean and 1:1: `agnews_article_metadata.article_id` covers all 127,600 articles; `agnews_authors.name` is unique, so filtering on the exact name is safe.
- `publication_date` is varchar, always 'YYYY-MM-DD', so string range comparisons work. Dates span 2004-01-01 to 2022-12-30 in every region.
- `region` has 5 continent values, each with about 25.4k–25.7k rows. Region totals are nearly equal, so a ranking of regions depends on classifying the category well. Return every region with its count, not only the top one.
- Category signals: a source tag in parentheses at the end of the title (about 18k titles have one). PC World, SPACE.com, Ziff Davis, InfoWorld, MacCentral, NewsFactor, TechWeb and SiliconValley.com mean Science/Technology. Forbes.com, Investor's Business Daily, TheDeal.com, The Motley Fool and FT.com mean Business. AP, Reuters, AFP, Canadian Press and UpdateN appear in every category and tell you nothing.
- Science/Technology covers computing, internet, software, telecom, space and science. A tech company's earnings or merger story is usually Business. Sports covers games, teams, athletes and the Olympics. World covers politics, conflict, diplomacy and disasters.
- For a small set of rows (for example one author's articles), SELECT every title+description, classify each row by meaning, and answer in derived mode. Keep a careful tally and check that the four category counts add up to the total.
- "Per year from Y1 to Y2 inclusive": divide by the number of calendar years (Y2−Y1+1). The window is `>= 'Y1-01-01'` and `< '(Y2+1)-01-01'`.
sessions.rationale: All three failures come from having to infer the category with no label column. The notes say this plainly and list the source tags I checked that signal Tech or Business. They also give the boundaries between categories and a careful per-row tally for small sets such as one author's articles (q2). The region and date facts I checked cover the windowing and per-year averaging (q3), and the warning about close region counts covers q4.

sessions.notes:
- Repo metrics (stars, forks, open issues) exist ONLY as free text in `deps_dev_v1_project_info."Project_Information"`. Take the `owner/repo` slug as the first slash-joined token (regex like `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]*[A-Za-z0-9_-]`), lowercase it, and join it to lowercased `deps_dev_v1_project_packageversion."ProjectName"`. Don't LIKE-match the whole text.
- Numbers can have thousands commas. Strip them, then cast to bigint.
- Forks come in 3 phrasings: "forks count of N", "forked N times", "N forks". Use coalesce over all three, case-insensitive.
- Stars: "stars count of N", "N stars", "starred by N users". Use all three.
- Open issues: "open issues count of N" or "N open issues".
- `Licenses` (project and package) and `VersionInfo` are JSON stored as text. Parse as jsonb (key-exists test for 'MIT'; read IsRelease and Ordinal as text, then cast). "Project license" means `project_info."Licenses"`.
- Join path: packageinfo(System,Name,Version) = project_packageversion(System,Name,Version), then ProjectName = slug.
- `VersionInfo` Ordinal is the registry's version order within a package. `UpstreamPublishedAt` (ms epoch) has nulls, and ordering by it picks a different top version than Ordinal for ~500 NPM release packages.
- One repo maps to many package names and versions (several repos have 75-900 NPM package names), so star/fork rankings over packages have large ties at equal values, and one project has many package-version rows.
